verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, of David, a psalm, a song.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, set down under David's name: a psalm to be played, a song to be sung.
verses.directors_commentary: This is a stage direction, not part of the poem. The KJV prints it as verse 0 and then its verse 1 is our verse 2, so every verse number in the English runs one behind the Hebrew. The word lamnatzeach is traditionally the leader of the temple musicians; the lamed in ledavid can mean 'by', 'for' or 'belonging to the collection of' David, and the KJV's 'A Psalm or Song of David' picks one. Mizmor (a piece with instruments) and shir (a sung piece) stand side by side; the KJV 'Psalm or Song' invents an 'or' that is not there. The medieval commentators cannot agree what battle lies behind it: Radak says Sennacherib's army, Meiri says Gog and Magog, Malbim says David's wars east of the Jordan.

philological_notes.note: 'To the leader' of the music; the root can mean 'be preeminent, supervise', and later 'victory'. The commentators here do not explain the word, only the setting of the psalm: Radak reads it as about Sennacherib, Meiri as Gog and Magog or the Exodus.

verses.translation_literal: May God arise; may his enemies be scattered, and may those who hate him flee from before him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let God rise. And at his rising, let his enemies break apart like a scattered flock; let all who hate him run, run from the sight of his face.
verses.directors_commentary: These are the words Moses said whenever the ark set out in the wilderness: 'Arise, YHWH, and let your enemies be scattered' (Num 10:35). The psalm opens by quoting the march-song of a camp on the move, so the first audience heard soldiers and desert tents before they heard anything else. The verbs are in the short, wishing form: this is prayer and prophecy at once, which is why Radak says it may be either. 'Arise' is what a warrior does when he gets up from his seat to fight, not a polite request. The KJV's 'Let God arise' is correct, but 'let them also that hate him flee' adds an 'also' that the Hebrew does not have; the two halves are a parallel pair (enemies / haters) and then a single verb of flight. Note the repeated 'from before him' (mipanav, literally 'from his face'): the enemy is routed by facing God, not by being hit.

philological_notes.note: 'Arise' is a warrior's verb: God gets up to act. Radak says the 'rising' is the display of his might, and that the verb may be prayer or prophecy. The words echo Num 10:35.
'Be scattered', driven apart in every direction, the opposite of an army in formation. Meiri: 'scattered hither and thither'.

verses.translation_literal: As smoke is driven off, you drive [them] off; as wax melts from before fire, the wicked perish from before God.
verses.translation_dramatic: Like smoke the wind takes, you take them; like wax at the edge of a flame, they run and soften and are gone. So the wicked perish, in the presence of God.
verses.directors_commentary: Two household images, smoke and a candle. Both were everyday things in an ancient house, where cooking fires and oil lamps filled every room: smoke vanishes with one gust, and beeswax (donag) goes from solid to puddle at the first heat. The point is not violence but weightlessness: the wicked have no substance when God is present. The Hebrew suddenly shifts from 'may they be scattered' to 'you drive them off', speaking to God directly in the second person; the KJV smooths this into a wish ('so drive them away'). The two lines are built on the same sound repeat, 'kehindof ... tindof' and 'kehimes', the infinitive of the thing and then the act, which the literal layer keeps by repeating 'driven off ... drive off'. Rashi hears the ark in the desert in 'before God'. Malbim notes that the pillar of fire and cloud that led Israel is turned into choking smoke and fire for their enemies.

philological_notes.note: Verbal noun of 'drive off', 'as the driving-off of smoke'. Ibn Ezra and Radak discuss whether it is a niphal or a hiphil infinitive; Rashi simply glosses it as 'as smoke is dispersed'. The verb is repeated in 'tindof' to make a sound pair.
Beeswax. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion gloss it simply as 'wax'.

verses.translation_literal: And the righteous, may they rejoice; may they exult before God, and may they be elated with joy.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the righteous. Let them be glad. Let them leap for joy in the very presence that melts the wicked; let them be lost in gladness.
verses.directors_commentary: The same 'before God' (lifnei) that dissolves the wicked now opens the door to the righteous: one presence, two results. Malbim says the light that is smoke to the wicked is cloud and shining to the righteous. The verse piles up three near-synonyms (smach, alatz, sus) and then a noun, simchah, so that the line itself bubbles over; Radak says the repetition shows how great the joy is. The KJV's 'yea, let them exceedingly rejoice' turns the last clause into an intensifier, but Hebrew says 'rejoice with joy', a cognate pair, the way English says 'sing a song'. 'The righteous' (tzaddikim) here are not the sinless but the loyal members of the covenant community; Ibn Ezra reads them as those with David and Radak as Hezekiah and Israel.

philological_notes.note: 'Exult', a strong, often physical, word for joy, close to 'jump for joy'. Metzudat Zion simply glosses it as 'a matter of gladness'.

verses.translation_literal: Sing to God, sing praise [to] his name; lift up [a way] for the rider through the steppes. In Yah is his name; and exult before him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Sing to God! Sing his name aloud. Build up the road for the one who rides across the open plains, whose name is Yah. And dance before his face.
verses.directors_commentary: The mood turns from the battlefield to worship, and the stage direction is to the congregation: Ibn Ezra says 'they will say to one another, sing to God'. Three verbs of praise (shiru, zameru, sollu) then one of exulting. The hard word is the phrase 'rider in the aravot'. The KJV's 'him that rideth upon the heavens' follows a tradition (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri) that aravot is a name for the high sky, and cites Deut 33:26, 'rider of the heavens'. YLT, ASV and BBE render it 'deserts', which fits the wilderness march that follows in verses 8-9, and also a verse of Isaiah (40:3) about a highway through the arabah. There is a further possibility, from Ugaritic poems where Baal is called 'rider of the clouds'. If so, this is polemic: the rider of the storm is not Baal but YHWH. That last point is my reading, unsourced. Solu is also double: 'raise him up in praise' (Rashi, Radak) or 'cast up a road' (Metzudat Zion, citing Isa 62:10). Yah is the short form of the divine name, which the KJV keeps as 'Jah' in the one place that name appears in its Psalms.

philological_notes.note: From 'raise up'. Two readings: 'extol' (Rashi, Radak, Ibn Ezra) or 'build up a highway' (Metzudat Zion, citing Isa 62:10; Malbim citing Isa 40:3).

Plural of 'steppe, arid plain' (the Arabah); the commentators read it as a name for heaven, the highest sphere that turns the others. The wilderness meaning suits the march-song of v. 8; the 'clouds' meaning is attested only as a conjecture.
Short form of the name YHWH. Rashi derives it from a word meaning 'awesome', after the Targum, and compares Isa 26:4.

verses.translation_literal: Father of the fatherless and judge of widows: God, in his holy dwelling.
verses.translation_dramatic: A father to those who have no father. A judge for the widows. This is God, in his holy dwelling place.
verses.directors_commentary: The one who rides the steppes is also the one who protects the weakest. In the ancient Near East a fatherless child and a widow had no man to defend them in court or to hold their land, so they were the first to be robbed. Kings boasted of defending them, and the Torah commands it. Here the claim is stronger: God is the father, and 'judge' (dayyan) is the one who actually decides the case, not merely hears it. The line is a nominal sentence with no verb ('Father ... and judge ... God'), and the KJV's 'is God in his holy habitation' reorders it to put God last, the same order the Hebrew has. Radak and Ibn Ezra stress the contrast of high and low: he is in his holy dwelling in the heavens, yet he is with the lowest on earth. Rashi reads the orphans and widows as Israel and Jerusalem, from Lamentations.

philological_notes.note: A judge who rules on the case and carries it out, not merely a bystander; the pair 'father of orphans, judge of widows' is the Bible's standard formula for God's justice for the powerless.
'His holy dwelling', heaven or the sanctuary. Metzudat Zion: 'a matter of residence'. Radak: although he is there, he is with the lowly on earth.

verses.translation_literal: God, causing the solitary to dwell [in] a household, bringing out prisoners into prosperity; only the rebellious dwell [in] a parched land.
verses.translation_dramatic: God gives the lonely a home, and the prisoners he leads out into the light of good days. But the stubborn, the ones who turn away, make their homes in a land of cracked and dry stone.
verses.directors_commentary: Three scenes: the isolated person gets a household, the captive is freed, and the rebel is left with a dry land. 'Solitary' (yechidim) means someone with no family; the KJV 'setteth ... in families' is a fair paraphrase, but Hebrew says bayta, literally 'homeward', 'to a house', and in biblical idiom 'house' means a family line and its property (as in 'he made them houses', Ex 1:21, quoted by Ibn Ezra and Radak). The next clause has a rare word, kosharot, found nowhere else. Rashi and Metzudat David take it as 'fitness': Israel left Egypt in Nisan, a season 'fit for travellers', neither hot nor cold. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri take it as 'fetters', by a letter-swap with 'bound'. The KJV picked fetters ('those which are bound with chains'), while the ASV/YLT pick 'prosperity', so the Bible reader has two verses depending on the translation. The closing line has a sting: 'only' (ach) and then the dry soil, tzechichah, bare sun-baked rock. The rebels are the ones left outside the household. Rashi says they are Egypt; Radak says Assyria.

philological_notes.note: A word found only here. Two ancient readings: 'in the right season' (Rashi, citing the Sifre; Metzudat David) or 'in chains' (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri, with the letter swap kaf/qof). Ibn Ezra compares 'kishor' in Prov 31:19.
Bare, sun-scorched rock, as in Ezek 24:7. Ibn Ezra: 'dryness, the opposite of dwelling in a household'.

verses.translation_literal: God, in your going out before your people, in your marching in the wasteland. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: O God, when you went out in front of your people, when you strode through the empty wilderness, step after step, where no road was. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: Here the psalm addresses God directly and looks back to the exodus. 'Going out before your people' is what a commander or a shepherd does, and in the march the ark and the pillar of cloud went ahead of the camp (Ibn Ezra, Metzudat David, the Targum). Tzaad is 'to take a step', a measured military stride, and the word is paired with yeshimon, the 'desolation', the waste where no one lives. Ibn Ezra insists that a place called 'desolation' cannot be Sinai itself, which was settled, but the wilderness after it. 'Selah' is a mark whose meaning is lost; the KJV leaves it untranslated, and so does the ASV in brackets. It probably signals a pause or a musical lift, and Rashi turns it into a statement: 'there you showed me that this is your way forever'. The KJV's 'Selah' ends the verse with a colon, which hides the fact that the sentence has no main verb; it is a heading for what comes next.

philological_notes.note: 'In your striding', the measured step of a marching person; Metzudat Zion: 'steps and paces'.
'Desolation', the uninhabited desert. Ibn Ezra uses it to argue that the verse cannot refer to Sinai, which was settled.
A musical or liturgical mark whose meaning is unknown. Rashi turns it into a comment: 'there you showed me that this is your way forever.'

verses.translation_literal: Earth quaked; also heavens dripped from before God; this Sinai, from before God, God of Israel.
verses.translation_dramatic: The earth shook. The very heavens poured down before God. Sinai itself, that mountain, trembled before the God of Israel.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the verse most like the old poems of Judges 5 and Deuteronomy 33: the earth quakes and the sky drips as the storm-God marches. 'Dripped' (natfu) is not necessarily rain; the KJV and ASV take it as raining, Metzudat David and Radak take it as a figure for fear or darkness over the enemy, and the Targum reads 'they let dew fall'. 'Earth' may mean the land or its peoples (Radak, Metzudat David). The middle phrase, 'zeh Sinai', is a curious, abrupt clause: 'this one, Sinai', the demonstrative a bit like a finger pointing at the mountain, a reference some scholars read as a gloss. The KJV's 'even Sinai itself was moved' adds a verb ('was moved') that the Hebrew does not have: it is just 'this Sinai'. The closing 'God of Israel' ties the storm to a particular people and not to a nature god, which was the point against Baal-worship.

philological_notes.note: 'They dripped'. Read as rain (KJV/ASV), as the drip of sweat from terror (Metzudat David), or as darkness over the enemy (Radak, Meiri citing Ps 18:12).
'This Sinai', a pointing phrase with no verb. Rashi adds that the mountain also quaked; Meiri connects Sinai to a word for burning.

verses.translation_literal: A rain of freewill gifts you shake out, God; your inheritance, and it weary, you yourself established it.
verses.translation_dramatic: A rain you gave freely, God, a rain of gifts shaken out like water from your hand. And your inheritance, worn out and parched, you set on its feet again.
verses.directors_commentary: In a land that lives on winter rain, a good rain is the gift that decides whether children eat. Geshem nedavot is a 'rain of free gifts': nedavah is a freewill offering, something given with no obligation. Metzudat David says: 'not by reward of deeds but as a free gift'. Malbim adds that in the settled land God is bound to send rain, but in the wilderness it is pure grace. The KJV says 'a plentiful rain', which makes it a matter of quantity; the Hebrew says it is a matter of generosity. 'You shook out' (tanif) is the same verb for shaking a sieve or waving an offering. The second half has an 'and it was weary' (venil'ah) that the KJV ('when it was weary') turns into a time clause; the Hebrew is looser: 'your inheritance, and weary, you set it up'. The 'inheritance' is Israel or its land (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Rashi), and the rain is a restoration, so the same word that says 'weary' in Jeremiah (20:9) says the land is worn out.

philological_notes.note: 'A rain of freewill gifts', rain given with no obligation. Metzudat David: 'not as a reward for deeds but as a free gift'. Rashi: 'rains of free gift and blessing'.
'You shake out', 'pour': Ibn Ezra glosses it 'you water', Metzudat Zion 'pour down, melt', with a comparison to a dripping honeycomb.

verses.translation_literal: Your living-band dwelt in it; you prepare in your goodness for the poor, God.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your own flock settled in that land. And out of your goodness, God, you laid a table for the poor.
verses.directors_commentary: Chayyah normally means 'a living creature, an animal', and here a 'herd' or 'band': Rashi and Metzudat Zion point to 2 Sam 23:11, where a chayyah is a company of Philistines. The KJV's 'congregation' keeps that sense but hides the image of a flock gathered by its shepherd, which Rashi in his second reading makes explicit: Israel is God's 'beast', his own creatures. The verb 'dwelt' is a past tense, but 'you prepare' is a present, a habitual verb: the first happened once, the second goes on. The poor (ani) are those with no land or protection, and what God prepares for them is food, or a place, from his 'goodness' (tovah, which means both kindness and the good things it brings). The KJV's 'prepared of thy goodness' adds an 'of' that makes it a share; the Hebrew says 'in your goodness', the way in which he prepares. Radak reads the poor as the exiled tribes.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'your living thing / your band'. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion read 'your congregation', citing 2 Sam 23:11. Rashi's second reading: Israel as God's own creature.

verses.translation_literal: My Lord gives a word; the women bearing news [are] a great host.
verses.translation_dramatic: The Lord speaks a word. And the women who carry the news, a great army of them, send it out.
verses.directors_commentary: Here the poem turns from rain to news. 'The Lord gives a word' is a command from the commander, and the answer is a crowd of women. The word translated 'those that published it' by the KJV is feminine plural: hamevasserot, 'the women who bring good news'. In ancient Israel women met returning armies with songs and drums (Exod 15:20-21, Judg 11:34, 1 Sam 18:6-7), so this is the victory announcement, and the 'host' (tzava) is the same word for an army, which makes the singing women a second army. The KJV's 'those that published it' removes the women; the ASV, YLT and BBE restore them. Ibn Ezra says the Lord will confirm the words of the women heralds in their songs. Radak says this is a great host of women who proclaim. The Targum has Moses and Aaron announcing instead, so the sense was disputed from the start. The title Adonai is rendered 'the Lord'; the text has the divine title and not the name.

philological_notes.note: Feminine plural participle with the article, 'the women who bear good news'. Metzudat Zion: 'from the word for tidings'. Radak and Ibn Ezra take it as women; the Targum says Moses and Aaron.
'A word, saying'; Rashi: 'a pronouncement'. The poetic form of the usual word for speech.

verses.translation_literal: Kings of armies, they flee, they flee, and the dweller of the house, she divides plunder.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the word goes out, and here is what it says: the kings come streaming back down the roads, no longer kings of anything, only men running, running, with the dust of their own armies behind them. And in the house where the women have waited all this time, someone steps forward and begins to share out what the fleeing left behind.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse is a battle report in miniature, and its engine is the doubled verb: yidodun yidodun, 'they flee, they flee'. English usually weakens it (KJV 'did flee apace', which adds a speed the Hebrew does not state); keep the stutter, because it is the sound of panic repeating. The 'kings of armies' are the commanders of the enemy hosts (Ibn Ezra and Malbim: 'kings of the hosts of the nations'). A point of my own, not of the verse: the phrase echoes the divine title 'YHWH of armies' (tzeva'ot), known from elsewhere in the Bible (1 Sam 17:45), and an audience that knew the title could hear the human 'lords of hosts' run while the real one does not. The second half turns to the home front. In the ancient Near East war was fought by men away from home, and plunder was shared out afterwards, in Israel by a rule that gave an equal share to those who stayed with the baggage (1 Sam 30:24, Num 31:27). The 'woman of the house' is nevat bayit, literally 'the one who dwells at home', and the singular may mean the whole community pictured as a woman, as Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak read it (Ibn Ezra: the congregation that stayed in Jerusalem). KJV 'she that tarried at home' is close; its 'divided' hides that the verb is imperfect in the Hebrew: she is dividing, it is going on now. Plunder, shalal, is the war-gain: cloth, metal, animals.

philological_notes.note: The repeated imperfect of nadad, 'to flee, wander off'. The doubling is emphatic, as if the verb itself were fleeing; most translations flatten it into one verb plus an adverb.

Construct of naweh, 'dwelling, pasture', here a person: the one who dwells at the house, the stay-at-home woman. It does not mean 'beautiful woman' (the STEPBible gloss mixes it with a different word, נָאוָה).

verses.translation_literal: If you lie down between the two saddlebags, the wings of a dove are covered with silver, and its pinions with greenish gold.
verses.translation_dramatic: You who have lain among the ashes and the sheepfolds, and slept close to the soot, look up: the wings of a dove, beaten over with silver, flash in the light, and under them the long feathers glint with a gold that is almost green.
verses.directors_commentary: This is among the hardest verses in the psalter, and the director should say so to the actors. The Hebrew has three problems at once. First, shefatayim, a dual form, which means 'two [something]'. The related form mishpetayim appears in Gen 49:14 (Issachar between the two) and Judg 5:16 (Reuben, listening to the flocks), where it seems to mean the loading of a pack animal or the pens of sheep; it is not the same word, so that parallel only suggests a meaning. The rabbis (Radak, Ibn Ezra, Metzudat Zion, comparing Ezek 24:3, 'rims of the pot') took shefatayim as the two stones on which a cooking pot is set, black with soot, so that 'to lie between them' is to sleep in the ashes, degraded. KJV 'among the pots' follows that; ASV 'sheepfolds' the other. Second, the verbs: 'you lie down' is plural and addressed to someone, but the line that follows is a bare description with no verb of its own, so the English 'though' and 'yet shall ye be' that KJV supplies are inference. Third, who is the dove? Israel (Rashi, Radak), or the people shown at last washed clean. The imagery is clear even if the logic is not: dull and dirty, then silver and gold. Yeraqraq, 'greenish', is a reduplicated colour word, a pale sheen, like adamdam 'reddish' in Lev 13:42 (Rashi): it is the colour of the best gold, which Radak and Meiri say is the greenish kind. Charuts is a poetic word for gold (Metzudat Zion). KJV 'yellow gold' loses the shimmer; BBE 'yellow gold' likewise. The order is inverted, 'greenish of gold' for 'gold of greenish' (Radak, Meiri). My own guess, with no source: a dove figure plated in precious metal would be a temple treasure, and that may be the image.

philological_notes.note: A dual of uncertain sense: 'hearth stones/pot rims' (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Metzudat Zion), 'saddlebags or pack-loads' or 'sheepfolds' (suggested by the related mishpetayim of Gen 49:14 and Judg 5:16, a different form). The dual suggests 'two' of something between which one can lie.

'With greenish gold': a reduplicated adjective, as in adamdam 'reddish' (Lev 13:42). Rashi explains it as the colour of the best Havilah gold, neither green nor red. Radak says the attribute stands for the thing described and the order is reversed; Meiri adds the parallel of Ps 89:51 for such an inverted phrase.

token_glosses.gloss: the two saddlebags (or hearth-stones, or sheepfolds)

verses.translation_literal: In the Almighty's scattering kings in it, let it snow on Zalmon.
verses.translation_dramatic: When the Almighty broke the kings apart like a spread cloth and flung them over that land, it was as if a snowfall came down on the dark hill of Zalmon: everything went white.
verses.directors_commentary: A verse of six words whose syntax defeats every translator. Beparés is an infinitive after 'in/when': 'in the scattering of'. The verb parás means to spread out, as one spreads a cloth, and so to scatter (Rashi compares Deut 22:17, 'they shall spread the garment'). KJV 'scattered' and ASV 'scattered' are right, but BBE 'put to flight' changes the picture: the image is of bodies or of an army strewn over a field. 'The Almighty' is Shaddai, a name of God from the patriarchal stories (Gen 17:1, Exod 6:3), an archaic and mountainous-sounding title (probably 'of the mountains', or 'the powerful one'), used here for the divine warrior. The kings are the same hosts of v13. Bah, 'in it', has no antecedent, and 'in it' is literally all the Hebrew gives: the land (Ibn Ezra), Jerusalem (Radak), or the battlefield. The last clause is a bare imperfect of the verb 'to snow', tashleg, with no subject and no 'as': the KJV 'it was white as snow' is an interpretation, supplying a comparison where the poet gives an event. Zalmon is a wooded height near Shechem (Judg 9:48), where Abimelech cut branches for fire, and so a hill known for darkness or shade, tsalmon, close to tsalmavet, 'deep darkness' (Rashi, Radak, Metzudat Zion). Whether the poet means white bones on a black mountain, a literal snowfall, or a wordplay on 'darkness', the audience hears the pun.

philological_notes.note: Infinitive construct: 'in the spreading out'. The verb is used for spreading cloth (Deut 22:17), spreading hands in prayer, and a bird spreading wings. For armies it means to disperse them as one spreads out a sheet.

The divine name 'Shaddai', usually 'Almighty' (a traditional rendering, perhaps ancient, from the Septuagint); its derivation is disputed ('mountain', 'breast', 'destroyer'). The name is archaic in a psalm of the divine warrior.
'It snows on Zalmon': the verb has no subject. The name is close to tsalmavet 'deep darkness', as Rashi, Radak and Metzudat Zion say; whether that is deliberate wordplay is not certain.

verses.translation_literal: A mountain of God, the mountain of Bashan; a mountain of many peaks, the mountain of Bashan.
verses.translation_dramatic: A mountain of God, they call it, the mountain of Bashan; a mountain heaped with summits, ridge on ridge, the mountain of Bashan.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse is built on four 'har', 'mountain', and a refrain, 'Bashan', that closes both halves. Read it as a chant, the way a pilgrim would sing the praise of a place. Bashan is the high basalt plateau east of the Sea of Galilee and the Jordan, with Mount Hermon at its north end; it was fertile, rain-watered grazing land, famous for its fat cattle ('cows of Bashan', Amos 4:1) and its oaks (Isa 2:13). It was a mountain of power and of the old gods: the Ugaritic texts place the divine assembly on mountains in the north, and so 'a mountain of God' (har elohim) can mean 'a mountain belonging to God' or simply 'a huge mountain', for elohim may add intensity, as in 'a mighty wind'. English readers should hear that this verse admires the very mountain which the next one will scorn, as a rival. KJV 'The hill of God is as the hill of Bashan' inserts 'as', turning a statement into a simile that the Hebrew does not have, and 'an high hill' softens gavnunim, an otherwise unattested word (a hapax) built on gav, 'back, hump': a mountain with humps, or ridges, many peaks (Rashi, Radak, Metzudat Zion). Many translators treat it as 'peaked, rugged', and the plural ending adds the sense that there is not one summit but a rolling crowd of them.

philological_notes.note: Hapax legomenon: 'many-peaked, humped'. It derives from gav 'back, rounded top' (compare Ezek 16:24, 'you built yourself a gav'). The ending -un can be a diminutive or a plural.
'Mountain of God': in the Hebrew phrase, elohim may mean the divine name or an intensifier ('a very great mountain'). Rashi and Radak identify the mountain as Sinai; the Targum, as Moriah.

verses.translation_literal: Why do you watch with envy, mountains of many peaks, the mountain God desired for his dwelling? Also YHWH will dwell for perpetuity.
verses.translation_dramatic: Why do you stare, you great ranges with all your crowded peaks, at the one small hill that God has chosen for his home? Yes, YHWH himself will live there, and live there for good.
verses.directors_commentary: The mountains of Bashan are suddenly addressed as people, with a sneer: 'Why do you glare?' The word is teratsedun, found only here, and the meaning is guessed from context and roots. Rashi's two sources offer 'lie in wait, ambush' (Arabic) and 'dance' (like r-q-d), and the KJV 'leap' follows the second. The modern consensus, and ASV, YLT and BBE, is 'look askance, with envy'. The picture is of tall mountains staring at the little hill on which God has chosen to live. This is the verse's irony: the tall mountains in the north, where the old gods were thought to sit, have nothing that God wants, and he chooses a low rise instead, Zion (the Targum names Sinai or Moriah, Rashi the Temple Mount). 'Desired' (chamad) is an emotionally strong verb: he coveted it, as in 'you shall not covet'. The verse is a polemic against the high places of surrounding religions, where gods were housed on lofty mountains such as Baal Zaphon. The second half names the God by the personal name YHWH and says he 'will dwell', yishkon, the verb that gives us shekhinah, 'the dwelling presence'. KJV renders the name 'the Lord' and the Hebrew 'perpetuity', netzach, as 'for ever', which is fair, and 'in it' is added; 'also' (af) has the sense of 'yes, even'.

philological_notes.note: Hapax, of uncertain meaning: 'look askance' or 'watch with envy' (the sense of a root known from Arabic), or 'dance, leap' as Menachem and the Targum read it. Rashi gives both.
'Desired, coveted': the verb of the tenth commandment, used here with God as subject, which makes the choice of the mountain an act of longing, not only of selection.

verses.translation_literal: The chariotry of God, twice ten thousand, thousands of repetition; the Lord is among them, Sinai in the holiness.
verses.translation_dramatic: God's chariots are beyond counting: tens of thousands, thousands upon thousands, wheel after wheel. And the Lord is in the midst of them, as he was at Sinai, in the holy place.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse piles numbers until the number gives out. Ribotayim is a dual: 'two myriads', twenty thousand. Alfei shin'an means 'thousands of shin'an', and that last word is a hapax, usually taken as 'repeating' (from shanah, 'to repeat, double'), so 'thousands upon thousands' (ASV) is the sense; the rabbis, followed by KJV 'angels', understood shin'an as a name for heavenly beings, probably because of the Aramaic 'sharp ones' (Rashi: sharp angels; Radak: 'the angels called shin'anim'). The chariots (rekhev, a collective: chariotry) are God's war machines, in the ancient Near East the most terrible weapon in the field, and the Bible shows God's chariot as a storm cloud (Ps 18:11, Hab 3:8) and, at Elisha's request, as horses and chariots of fire (2 Kgs 6:17, which Ibn Ezra and Meiri cite). The second half is elliptical, with no verb: 'the Lord among them, Sinai in the holiness', where English must add 'is'. KJV 'as in Sinai, in the holy place' adds 'as'. The audience should hear that Sinai has come to Zion: the holy mountain of the first revelation is present in the sanctuary, so God has not left the desert but brought his mountain with him. Note too the shift in divine title from Elohim to Adonai, 'my lord', the title of a king.

philological_notes.note: A hapax. Read as 'repetition, doubling' (from shanah), giving 'thousands upon thousands', or as 'angels' (Rashi: sharp, i.e. keen ones; Radak; Metzudat Zion). The Hebrew gives only the root-based form.
Dual of ribbo, 'myriad, ten thousand': 'two myriads', 'twenty thousand'. Ibn Ezra compares 'many myriads' around Elisha (2 Kgs 6:17).

verses.translation_literal: You went up to the height, you took captivity captive, you took gifts among humankind, and even rebels, to dwell, Yah God.
verses.translation_dramatic: You have gone up to the height, and you have taken your prisoners in a long line behind you. You have received gifts from among humankind, even from the stubborn, from those who rebelled, that Yah, God, may make his home among them.
verses.directors_commentary: The ascent of a victorious king: he goes up the mountain with his captured prisoners and receives tribute. This is how the ancient Near East staged victory, and the psalm's audience would have pictured the procession climbing to the sanctuary. Three points. First, 'you took captivity captive' (shavita shevi) is a cognate pair, 'you captured captives', and KJV 'led captivity captive' is a good echo. Second, the Hebrew says that the king took gifts baadam, 'among humankind' or 'in the human' (the preposition bet may mean 'from among' or 'in the form of': human beings as the gifts). KJV 'for men' is an interpretive change, and Paul in Ephesians 4:8 cites the verse as 'he gave gifts to men', following the Aramaic and Syriac tradition; the Hebrew says 'took'. Rashi and the Targum make the one who ascends Moses, who went up to heaven and took the Torah captive from the angels to give it to humankind; this reads the verb as 'taking' in order 'to give'. Radak and Meiri take the verse as a lament about exile. Third, the last clause has no stated subject: 'and even rebels, to dwell, Yah God': the rebels are brought so that God may dwell, with them or among them (Rashi: God dwelt in the tabernacle among a rebellious people). Soririm, 'rebels', has the sense of a stubborn calf that will not take the yoke (Hos 4:16). Yah is the short form of the divine name, found in 'hallelu-yah'. KJV 'Lord God' blurs the two names, Yah and Elohim.

philological_notes.note: A cognate accusative: 'you captured a capture', 'you led captives'. Rashi reads it as Moses taking the Torah captive.
'Among humankind' or 'in/as the human': a gift in the form of persons or taken from persons. The Hebrew does not say 'for men'; the sense 'gave to men' is from the Targum (Eph 4:8 follows it).
Participle: 'stubborn, rebellious ones'; of a calf or a son that will not obey (Hos 4:16, Deut 21:18). Rashi: the people in the wilderness; Radak: the king of Assyria.

verses.translation_literal: Blessed [be] the Lord, day by day he carries a load for us, the God of our salvation. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Blessed be the Lord! Day after day he takes up the weight and carries it for us, the God who is our rescue. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: After the thunder of the procession, a quiet turn: the voice of the community, thanking. The verb is the surprise. Yamas is 'to lift a load, to load up', used of a donkey carrying a burden or a man bearing a pack (Gen 44:13, Isa 46:3, 'borne by me from the womb'). It has no object here, and traditional commentators supply 'his blessings' (Radak, Metzudat David), which is how KJV came to say 'daily loadeth us with benefits'. But the verb in the Hebrew is the other way round: God does the carrying, and we are the ones whose burden he lifts. That is a different image of God from the chariot. Yom yom, 'day day', is an idiom for 'every single day', and KJV 'daily' catches that. 'The God of our salvation' (ha'el yeshuatenu) is 'the God, our salvation', with the definite article, and has the force of 'the God who is our deliverance'. 'Selah' appears at the end: a liturgical marker of unknown meaning, probably a pause or lifting of voices or instruments, which the actors should treat as a beat of silence. Here the 'Lord' is Adonai, not YHWH.

philological_notes.note: 'He loads, he lifts a burden': used of beasts of burden and of God carrying his people (Isa 46:3). The missing object is supplied as 'his blessings' by Radak and Metzudat David, but Malbim and Radak's alternative read 'our salvation' as the object.

verses.translation_literal: The God of us is a God of saving acts, and to YHWH the Lord belong escapes to death.
verses.translation_dramatic: Our God is a God who saves, again and again. And yet the doors that lead out into death are his too, the Lord YHWH's, and no one else's.
verses.directors_commentary: A two-sided verse: God of rescues, and master of death. The first line has the plural motsha'ot, 'saving acts, deliverances', which stresses that there are many. The second line's final phrase, lamavet totsa'ot, is hard. Totsa'ot, from yatsa 'to go out', means 'outgoings, exits', and in Prov 4:23 it is the 'wellsprings' of life; so 'exits to death' can mean 'ways out of death' (rescue), which is how ASV and YLT take it ('escape from death'), or 'exits that lead to death': the many ways God has to kill (Rashi, Radak, Malbim). KJV 'issues from death' is an archaic English that conceals this fork, and a modern reader will not see 'issues' as 'exits'. The context gives the second sense a certain weight because the next verse says what God does to enemies, but the parallel with 'God of saving acts' leans towards the first; the actor does not need to decide, because the line works as a hinge. Note also the doubled title in the Hebrew, YHWH Adonai, 'the Lord YHWH', a form that the Masoretes vocalised so that a reader would say 'Elohim' and avoid pronouncing the name, which is why some versions print 'GOD' in capitals. The sense that death has 'gates' (Ps 9:13) belongs to the world of the verse: Sheol as a place with exits and entrances.

philological_notes.note: 'Outgoings, exits': ways out. With lamavet ('to death') it is ambiguous between 'exits from death' and 'exits to death'; Rashi, Radak and Malbim take the second.
Plural of a rare noun: 'saving acts, deliverances'; the plural means that God's help is repeated and various.

verses.translation_literal: Surely God will shatter the head of his enemies, the scalp of hair, one who goes about in his guilts.
verses.translation_dramatic: But God, God alone, will break the heads of his enemies, the crown of hair on the man who goes on walking in his guilt, and does not turn.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the verse that the modern reader most wants to soften, and the English versions do. The Hebrew verb yimchats is violent: to crush, smash, pierce through (Judg 5:26 of Jael, Hab 3:13), and the BBE 'will be crushed' keeps this while the KJV 'wound' makes it a mild thing. The object, 'head', is then repeated in a second noun, the 'scalp of hair', kodkod se'ar, the crown where the hair parts (Radak): the poet wants the picture of a skull split at the very crown, in a hairy, i.e. long-haired or hirsute, warrior. KJV's 'hairy scalp' is exact, but the 'such an one as goeth on still' is a paraphrase of the habitual participle mithalekh, 'one who keeps on walking about'. Rashi hears Esau, 'the hairy man' (Gen 27:11), in 'hair', and reads the verse as a rabbinic allusion; the plain sense is the enemy warrior. The theology is of retribution: the target is the one who goes on in his guilt (ashamav, plural, 'his guilts, offences') without turning back. Ancient war language thought of the head as the seat of life and strength, and crushing the head is also the sentence of a divine warrior in Hab 3:13 and Gen 3:15. The opening word 'akh, 'surely, only', puts the weight on God alone doing it, as Radak says: without sword or spear.

philological_notes.note: 'Scalp of hair', the top of the head where the hair parts (Radak, Meiri). Rashi reads 'hairy' as Esau, the hairy man (Gen 27:11).
'Smash, shatter'; a strong verb for a head-blow, cf. Judg 5:26 and Hab 3:13. Metzudat Zion: striking and breaking.

verses.translation_literal: The Lord has said: From Bashan I will bring back, I will bring back from the depths of the sea.
verses.translation_dramatic: The Lord has spoken. From Bashan, high on its hills, I will bring them back; I will bring them back from the deep places of the sea.
verses.directors_commentary: God himself speaks now, in the first person, and the two promises are the two ends of the world as the psalmist knew it: the highest, wooded plateau of Bashan to the north-east, and the deepest, the maelstrom of the sea. The verb ashiv, 'I will bring back', is doubled, as in v13: God says it twice because he means it. English readers should note that the Hebrew has no object. KJV and Webster supply 'my people' in italics; ASV 'them'; the Hebrew leaves open whether it is Israelites to be fetched home from exile, or the enemies to be hauled out of their hiding places for judgment (the commentators split: Rashi, Meiri and Metzudat David say the exiles; Ibn Ezra, Radak and Malbim the enemies). The structure, height and depth, is a merism, like heaven and earth: from everywhere. 'Depths of the sea' (metsulot yam) is the language of the Exodus story, 'they sank into the depths like a stone' (Exod 15:5), and so Radak connects it with Egypt in the sea. The verb is in the first person, which matches the voice the psalm gives to Adonai in the preceding verse as the one 'to whom belong the escapes'. KJV 'The Lord said', as a past, is acceptable; the Hebrew perfect amar is a declaration whose effect continues, 'he has said'.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil imperfect 'I will bring back, restore'. It has no stated object. Rashi and Meiri supply the exiles; Ibn Ezra and Radak the enemies. The doubling emphasises resolve.
'From the depths of the sea', the deep water where things sink, cf. Exod 15:5, Jonah 2:4. Metzudat Zion: 'the deep of the sea'.

verses.translation_literal: So that it may smash, your foot, in blood, the tongue of your dogs, from enemies, its portion.
verses.translation_dramatic: So that your foot may be stained red in the blood, and the tongues of your dogs may have their share of it, a portion taken from the enemy.
verses.directors_commentary: The most graphic line of the window, and the English must not look away. It is a victory song, and it ends in a battlefield. The foot is 'smashed' or 'crushed' in blood, that is, you wade through it until your foot breaks through (Rashi, comparing Judg 5:26), and the dogs lap it. KJV 'dipped' and BBE 'red' make the image tidy; the verb timchats is the same root as yimchats in v22, 'shatter', so the poet may be echoing it: God will 'smash' the head, and the foot 'smashes' in the blood. Some saw a difficulty here: Radak, Meiri and, in Ibn Ezra, R. Yehudah read timchats as an inverted form of chamots, 'redden' (cf. Isa 63:1, 'red of garments'), which is the sense behind KJV 'dipped' and BBE 'red'. A modern emendation reads tirchats, 'bathe'; that is outside the packet and no commentator here gives it. Dogs in the ancient Near East were not pets but scavenger animals that ate the unburied dead, and an unburied corpse eaten by dogs was the worst of fates (1 Kgs 21:23, Jer 15:3). 'Your dogs' makes them God's own, the ministers of his judgment. The final word minehu, 'its portion', is rare; it means a share, from manah 'to apportion', as in Dan 1:10, 'he has apportioned your food' (Rashi), and Metzudat Zion links it to the food-word 'man' of Exod 16:15. KJV 'in the same' ignores the word. Radak and Meiri also read it as a repeat for emphasis, 'from the enemy', after 'from enemies'.

philological_notes.note: 'It may smash': read with Rashi as 'break through' the blood (as in Judg 5:26). Radak, Meiri and R. Yehudah in Ibn Ezra take it as an inverted form of chamots, 'redden' (cf. Isa 63:1).

'Its portion, share': from manah 'to apportion'. Rashi and Metzudat Zion link it to the 'man' (food ration) of Dan 1:10 and Exod 16:15. Ibn Ezra and Meiri offer other readings, such as 'from him' (miMenu).

verses.translation_literal: They have seen your processions, O God, the processions of my God, my king, in the holy place.
verses.translation_dramatic: They have seen you come, O God. They have seen the slow, unhurried march of my God, my king, as he passes into the holy place.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood changes here. The war is over and the poem shows a procession. The word הֲלִיכוֹת (halikhot, 'goings') is the same word a king's march would be called: the steady, public walking of a ruler with his people lining the road. The psalm has been following God as he marches through the desert and the storm (68:8-9, 18); here the viewers finally see it, and the scene is a liturgy. Notice the person: the verse starts with 'your' (you, O God) and ends with 'my God, my king'. The worshipper moves from a formal address to a personal claim, as if the voice leaps from the crowd.

KJV 'in the sanctuary' is right but narrow: בַּקֹּדֶשׁ is only 'in the holy', a place or a state, and the old commentators argue about whether it means the temple (Radak: the holy heaven), the sea crossing (Rashi: 'in your holiness, at the sea') or the holy land (Malbim). ASV's 'into the sanctuary' and BBE's 'into the holy place' take the preposition as motion, which the Hebrew does not say. The tradition places the scene at the Red Sea (Rashi, Metzudat David, Targum) or at the return to the land (Malbim); the Hebrew does not fix it. Direct the actor to look, not to point: 'they have seen' is the perfect of recognition.

philological_notes.note: A noun 'goings', 'processions', 'marches'; used for the way a king or caravan moves (Nah 2:6, Job 6:19). It stresses the visible walking of a person, not an abstract 'way'. The word is repeated in the second half of the verse for emphasis.
'In the holy (place)'. Commentators read it as the sanctuary, the heaven (Ibn Ezra, Radak) or the Red Sea crossing (Rashi).

verses.translation_literal: The singers went in front, after them the strikers of strings, in the midst of young women beating tambourines.
verses.translation_dramatic: The singers lead the way, their voices rising first. The players come behind them, and in the midst of it all, young women beat their tambourines, and the beat goes through the street like a pulse.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a parade with a fixed order: voices first (שָׁרִים, shārim, the singers), then those who play (נֹגְנִים), with girls drumming in the middle. It is the picture of a festival or a royal return, and a cultic one: women with hand-drums were the usual way to greet a returning warrior (Exod 15:20; Judg 11:34; 1 Sam 18:6). The tradition ties it to Miriam at the sea (Rashi, Metzudat David, Targum).

KJV's 'damsels' is archaic; the Hebrew עֲלָמוֹת is young women of marrying age, and the word does not say 'virgin' (YLT's choice). KJV 'timbrels' is a good old word for the tambourine-like frame drum. BBE's 'brass instruments' is simply wrong: תֹּף is a skin drum. The participle תּוֹפֵפוֹת is a verb form of the noun תֹּף: 'drumming', and the repeated 'p-p' sound imitates the beat. Do not rush the stage direction; the three groups must read as a moving line.

philological_notes.note: Young women of marriageable age, the same word as in Isa 7:14 and in the heading of Ps 46. It states age and status, not sexual history. KJV's 'damsels' keeps the right sense; YLT's 'virgins' does not translate the word.

A participle 'beating a drum', formed from תֹּף 'frame drum'. The doubled consonant sounds like the beat. Ibn Ezra and Radak discuss the form, with Radak calling it a descriptive adjective like שׁוֹמֵמוֹת.

verses.translation_literal: In assemblies bless God, YHWH, from the fountain of Israel.
verses.translation_dramatic: In the great gatherings, bless God. Bless the LORD, all you who spring from the well of Israel.
verses.directors_commentary:
The procession turns into a command: the singers now address the crowd, and the crowd is called a 'fountain'. The image is of descent: a people as water, flowing from one spring, the ancestor Jacob (the Targum and Rashi hear the unborn children, still in the womb, singing; Ibn Ezra compares Isa 48:1, 'out of the waters of Judah'). Ancient Israelite worship was communal and public: מַקְהֵלוֹת (maqhelot) are the plural 'assemblies', a rare word that occurs again only in Ps 26:12. The verse puts two divine names side by side, Elohim and YHWH, with no conjunction between them: 'God, YHWH', which is why KJV's 'even the Lord' is a smoothing; the Hebrew has an apposition, and a reader should hear the name said aloud.

KJV also writes 'the Lord' for the divine name, the standard softening of YHWH. In the literal layer we keep YHWH. KJV's 'ye ... from the fountain' attaches the clause to an imaginary 'ye that are of' (ASV adds this), but the Hebrew only has the preposition: 'from the fountain of Israel'. Most commentators take it as the origin of the blessers (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri, Metzudat David); Malbim reads it as the place of the blessing, the land of Israel.

philological_notes.note: 'From the fountain of Israel': the people as a spring and its descendants as its water. Most commentators take it to mean 'you who come from Israel's source' (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri, Metzudat David); Malbim takes it as the land of Israel, the place of the blessing.

verses.translation_literal: There Benjamin the little, ruling them; the princes of Judah, their stone-heap; the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali.
verses.translation_dramatic: And there they are, tribe by tribe: Benjamin, small as it is, in front, leading them. The princes of Judah come with their crowd around them. Then the princes of Zebulun, and the princes of Naphtali.
verses.directors_commentary:
The parade now has a roll call of four tribes: two from the south (Benjamin, Judah) and two from the far north (Zebulun, Naphtali). That a poem about Israel's God names tribes from both ends of the land is part of its claim: every part of the people has come. The first tribe is the smallest, and the surprise is deliberate: little Benjamin leads. The psalm may remember Saul, the first king, who came from Benjamin (Rashi, Metzudat David, citing the old tradition on 1 Sam 15:17); others say Benjamin is the leader because the poem sees a procession in which the order is not by size.

The text is hard. רֹדֵם looks like 'ruling them' but has an odd vowel (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Meiri note it). The second phrase, רִגְמָתָם, occurs only here. KJV 'their council', ASV the same, YLT 'their defence' and BBE 'their army' all invent a meaning; the root רגם means to throw stones, so the word may be a 'heap', a 'throng' (a crowd that pelts the road with palm leaves?) or the pelting itself (Rashi, Metzudat David: stoning in jealousy). The tradition's reading, in which the other tribes threw stones at Judah, is alien to the surrounding praise; I would play it as a crowd. Zebulun and Naphtali are the northern tribes who stood with Deborah (Judg 5:18), which is why they are named last.

philological_notes.note: A hapax. The root means 'to throw stones' (Lev 20:2); the noun might be 'pile of stones', 'throng' or 'pelting'. Rashi and Metzudat David read 'stone-throwers', Radak 'their gathering'; KJV 'council' has no basis in the root.
'Little, small, youngest'. Rashi and Radak take it as the smallest of the tribes; Ibn Ezra also allows 'small in number'. STEPBible's 'insignificant' is too strong.

verses.translation_literal: Your God has commanded your strength. Be strong, O God, this which you have done for us.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your God has called forth your strength. Show it again, O God. Make strong what you have already made for us.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice drops from the pageant into prayer. It is brief and tense, and the whole line is built on one root, עזז 'to be strong': 'your strength' (עֻזְּךָ) and 'be strong!' (עוּזָּה). The pun asks the actor to lean on the sound. The speaker addresses Israel first ('your God ... your strength'), and then turns to God ('O God'): the order of speakers shifts in the middle of the verse, as in the famous prayer at the ark (Num 10:35, Rashi connects it to 'let God arise', Ps 68:2).

KJV 'Thy God hath commanded thy strength: strengthen, O God, that which thou hast wrought for us' is close, but it smooths two things. First, the verb is the imperative of a rare form, 'show strength!', not 'strengthen'. Second, זוּ (zu) is an old relative, 'this/which', which gives a poetic roughness. BBE rewrites the verse ('send out your strength'). Radak and Meiri note that the spelling of עוּזָּה is itself unusual, with vav and dagesh. Play it as a request and a reminder: what has already been done is the guarantee for what is asked.

philological_notes.note: Imperative 'be strong! show your strength!'. The spelling with vav and dagesh is unusual, which Radak and Meiri both note. It echoes עֻזְּךָ in the same verse.
A poetic relative or demonstrative: 'this (which)'. It points back to the deeds of the procession.

verses.translation_literal: From your temple over Jerusalem, to you kings will bring a gift.
verses.translation_dramatic: From your temple, high above Jerusalem, kings will come. They will bring their gifts to you.
verses.directors_commentary:
A short verse and a large claim: this is the first mention of the temple and the city in the poem. Foreign kings bringing a שַׁי (shay, 'gift') is the language of tribute, the payment a smaller state makes to a stronger one. Here it is made to a God, not a king, which is the polemic: the capital of the empire is the shrine, and the gods of the surrounding peoples do not receive tribute from the kings of the world (compare Isa 18:7, where the same word is used, as Metzudat Zion notes).

KJV 'Because of thy temple at Jerusalem' turns מִן (from) into a cause, which Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David also do. But the Hebrew only says 'from your temple', a direction of power and of splendour, which then reaches 'over Jerusalem'. The preposition עַל may mean 'above' or 'at'. BBE gives only half of the verse: 'Out of your Temple in Jerusalem.' Note that the verb is imperfect and hiphil, 'will bring/cause to be carried': the verse expects, not reports. The gift is carried (יוֹבִילוּ), not simply given: the picture is of a line of porters.

philological_notes.note: A gift brought to a superior, usually foreign tribute or a gift of honour (Isa 18:7). Metzudat Zion cites Isa 18:7.
Hiphil of יבל 'to bring, carry along'; it describes a procession of carriers. It is the same root as the 'jubilee' idea of 'ram's horn' in other contexts, but not here.

verses.translation_literal: Rebuke the beast of the reed, the herd of bulls with the calves of the peoples, trampling on bars of silver. He has scattered peoples; wars they delight in.
verses.translation_dramatic: Rebuke the beast of the reeds, the herd of mighty bulls and the calves of the nations, who stamp on bars of silver. He has scattered the peoples who love war.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the most difficult verse of the section and the one the translators fought over. It is a bestiary: the 'beast of the reed' (חַיַּת קָנֶה) might be the crocodile or hippopotamus, which means Egypt (many modern scholars take it so; Rashi names Amalek and Metzudat David Ishmael), or else the 'spearmen' (reed = lance, Ibn Ezra and Radak). The 'herd of bulls' (עֲדַת אַבִּירִים) are rulers and warriors, 'strong ones' with 'calves of the peoples', their followers (Radak: kings and nobles; Ibn Ezra compares 'the bulls of Bashan', Ps 22:13). KJV chose 'company of spearmen' and put the English in the court: this is a harmonized guess, and it hides the animals which the Hebrew has.

The ancient audience would hear Egyptian symbols in all of it, since Egypt was the land of the Nile reed beds and the bull-god Apis, and 'calves' would sound like idols. Then the next line: מִתְרַפֵּס בְּרַצֵּי־כָסֶף. The verb רפס means 'to trample' or to be trampled and the hithpael is 'to trample oneself' (to prostrate, Prov 6:3). The noun רַצֵּי is 'pieces' or 'bars', cognate with רצץ 'to crush', so KJV 'submit himself with pieces of silver' (also Rashi, Radak, Meiri: the enemy comes cringing, paying tribute) and ASV 'trampling under foot the pieces of silver' (the enemy treading on the silver of its own loot) are both possible. I kept 'trampling on' as the literal; the other reading is equally strong. The verb בִּזַּר is a perfect, 'he has scattered', with no stated subject, so the end is a statement that breaks the imperatives: KJV's 'scatter thou' alters the grammar. 'Delight in wars' keeps the vocabulary of pleasure: חָפֵץ.

philological_notes.note: 'The beast of the reed' (or, with Ibn Ezra and Radak, the 'company of lances', since קנה can mean 'spear shaft'). It is probably an image of a river animal and hence of Egypt, but the verse does not say so. Rashi names Amalek by Ps 80:14, Metzudat David Ishmael.
A hithpael participle, 'trampling oneself' or 'being trampled', i.e. grovelling. The root also gives Dan 7:7, 'trampled'. The metaphor is of a beaten foe coming to pay.
'Pieces / bars of silver', as Radak and Meiri say (from 'crush'). Ancient silver was paid as scrap, weighed out in pieces, not as coin; the image is of tribute.

verses.translation_literal: Nobles will come from Egypt; Cush will make its hands run to God.
verses.translation_dramatic: From Egypt the nobles will come, and Cush will make her hands run to God.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the beasts, the former enemies arrive as pilgrims. Egypt and Cush (Nubia, south of Egypt, what the KJV calls 'Ethiopia') are at the far edge of the known world and at the height of their power, and a gift from them is the sign of the highest honour. The poem states the reverse of the exodus: Egypt, the house of slavery, now sends envoys.

The word חַשְׁמַנִּים (chashmannim) occurs only here, and the versions guess: 'princes' (KJV, ASV, Webster), 'fat ones' (YLT, from a related root), 'envoys' (STEPBible), and BBE adds Pathros and silver, which are not in the Hebrew. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri link it to the later name Hasmonean, in the sense of 'notable', and Rashi reports the alternative that it is a place name. The picture of Cush 'making its hands run' is unusual: the verb is hiphil, 'cause to run' (רוּץ), and the hands are the subject of the speed. KJV 'soon stretch out her hands' softens it twice: it makes the race into a stretching, and the haste into 'soon'. Radak points out the oddity that hands, not feet, run: because the hands carry the gift. Let the actor run with open hands.

philological_notes.note: A hapax of unknown meaning. The tradition reads 'notables, leaders' (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri, Metzudat Zion, linking it to Hasmonean). Rashi also reports Menachem's view that it is a place name.

Hiphil 'cause to run'. Hands run because they bring the gift (Radak), or because the body runs and the hands go with it (Metzudat David). A feminine verb with a masculine suffix, which Meiri explains as a shift between land and people.

verses.translation_literal: Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing praises to the Lord. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God! Sing praises to the Lord. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
The invitation becomes universal. After the tribes of Israel and the envoys of two nations, every kingdom is called. It is a call to a choir: two imperatives, שִׁירוּ and זַמְּרוּ, one for 'sing', the other for 'make music', which are used for singing with instruments; the verse repeats the first command of the psalm (68:5, 'sing to God, make music to his name').

The name here is אֲדֹנָי (Adonai, 'my Lord'), not the divine name YHWH. KJV marks the difference only by typography: 'Lord' for Adonai, 'LORD' in small capitals for YHWH. That distinction lives on the page and is lost when the verse is read aloud, so a listener cannot tell the two titles apart; the Hebrew ear could. סֶלָה (Selah) is a marker whose meaning is uncertain: probably a pause or a musical instruction, such as a rise or an interlude. KJV and YLT keep it, while BBE puts it in brackets. Let the actor treat it as a breath: the section ends, the singing stops, and the next verse starts from a different place (the sky).

philological_notes.note: A liturgical or musical marker of unknown meaning, often taken as a pause or an interlude. It marks the end of a section here.

verses.translation_literal: To the rider in the heavens of the heavens of ancient time. Behold, he gives with his voice a voice of strength.
verses.translation_dramatic: To him who rides the heavens, the heavens of heavens, as old as time. Listen: he lifts his voice, and it is a voice of power.
verses.directors_commentary:
The camera lifts. The psalm began with God as the 'rider' (68:5); here it makes the claim again, and a storm is coming. Everything in the sentence pushes upward: the double 'heavens of heavens' is the Hebrew superlative, the highest heaven, and 'ancient' (קֶדֶם) makes it as old as the creation. The 'voice' is thunder, and the psalmist uses the same word (קוֹל) twice in one breath: 'with his voice a voice of strength', so the actor should let the word return like thunder.

The polemic is my own reading, and none of the commentaries in the packet makes it: 'rider' echoes a title of the storm god Baal in the Ugaritic poems, and for those who know Canaan's religion the thunder and the clouds belong here to Yahweh, not to Baal. KJV 'doth send out his voice, and that a mighty voice' interprets 'gives' as 'send out', which is fine, and adds 'and that' to turn the repetition into emphasis. KJV's 'which were of old' reads 'of old' as a clause about the heavens, which is probably right, since Radak and Metzudat David say the heavens are the oldest of creations; Ibn Ezra says there is a hidden meaning. 'Behold' (הֵן) is a pointing word: the verse calls the audience to look and listen.

philological_notes.note: 'The heavens of the heavens of antiquity': the highest heaven, of ancient time. Radak and Metzudat David read 'the heavens above the heavens which God created in old times'. קדם also means 'east', which is lexically possible.

verses.translation_literal: Give strength to God. Over Israel [is] his majesty, and his strength [is] in the skies.
verses.translation_dramatic: Give strength to God. His majesty rests on Israel, and his might is in the skies.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice of thunder is answered by the worshippers: 'give strength to God'. This is an odd request, and the actor should play it so: nothing can be added to God's strength, so 'to give' it is to declare, ascribe, attribute it (Ibn Ezra: to acknowledge in words; Radak: to say it was his strength, not yours, that defeated the enemy). Metzudat Zion reads תְּנוּ as 'tell', as in Judg 5:11. The verse has two places: Israel (below) and the sky (above); majesty rests on one and strength in the other, and the vav is a link: 'as it is seen in the sky, so it is seen on Israel' (Radak). Ibn Ezra adds why Israel: they are his treasured people, and on them his majesty shows.

KJV 'his excellency is over Israel' uses 'excellency' for גַּאֲוָה, which is a surprising word. In the Hebrew Bible it is also 'pride' (Prov 8:13), but here it means the majesty of a king in splendour (compare Exod 15:7). KJV also changes the sense of בַּשְּׁחָקִים (the fine dust of the skies, the thin clouds) into the more general 'clouds', and BBE paraphrases 'make clear that strength is God's'. The distance is also the point: his strength is high and far, his majesty is on the people.

philological_notes.note: 'His majesty, his exaltation'. The word is often 'pride' in a bad sense, but with God it is the proper splendour of the king (compare Exod 15:7). KJV 'excellency' is acceptable but obscure. This is my own reading of the word's range, not a citation.
'Give strength': ascribe, declare it to be God's. Ibn Ezra reads it as confession in words; Radak as a statement that victory came from God's strength and not from yours.

verses.translation_literal: Awesome [is] God from your sanctuaries, God of Israel; he [is] giving strength and powers to the people. Blessed [be] God.
verses.translation_dramatic: Awesome is God, O Israel, as he comes from your sanctuaries. The God of Israel, he is the one who gives strength and power to his people. Blessed be God.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends as it began, with a blessing, and with a verb of fear: נוֹרָא (nora') is 'to be feared', 'awe-inspiring', not 'terrible' (KJV), where the old English word still means 'inspiring terror'. Now, 'terrible' has the modern sense of 'bad', so the audience hears the wrong thing.

The awe flows from the מִקְדָּשִׁים, 'sanctuaries', plural. KJV 'holy places' and ASV likewise. The plural is a puzzle that the tradition solves in different ways: the heavenly and the earthly temple, matching each other (Radak, Ibn Ezra); the three parts of the temple, porch, hall and inner room (Radak); or the plural of majesty. Rashi gives a midrash (reading מְקֻדָּשֶׁיךָ: 'from your sanctified ones') and a hard reading in which God is awesome because he destroyed even his own temple. Do not choose: let the actor say it in the plural and in the majesty of the place.

The final word on strength: the verb is a participle (נֹתֵן, 'is giving'), a present and continuing gift, and the two nouns עֹז and תַּעֲצֻמוֹת are a pair, 'strength' and 'powers' (the plural of intensity). The word the psalm keeps repeating, strength, is the last thing God gives. The poem ends with בָּרוּךְ אֱלֹהִים, 'blessed be God': in the Hebrew it is a statement, a cry of the crowd, not an order.

philological_notes.note: Plural 'your sanctuaries'. Explained as the temple above and below (Radak, Ibn Ezra), the three parts of the temple (Radak), or the plural of majesty. Rashi's midrash reads 'from your holy ones'.
'Powers, might'. A rare plural noun of abstract force, from the root of 'bone' and 'mighty'; with עֹז it forms a pair for emphasis (Metzudat Zion: from עצמה, strength).
